explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. He says, "O Lord, hear my voice; let Your ears be attentive to my plea for mercy." He's down in the depths and he doesn't show up with a speech. He just asks for mercy, plain and simple. I respect that, because I've never once gotten out of a tight spot by sounding fancy.

I get why you'd pick it, since this is a song, after all. But the writer isn't down there celebrating anything. He cries "Out of the depths I cry to You, O LORD!" and what he asks the LORD to hear is his "…plea for mercy." That's the cry, friend, and it's what the verse says.

Nice try, baker, but nobody in this song walks in waving a résumé. The writer asks the LORD's ears to be "…attentive to my plea for mercy." You don't ask for mercy by showing off what you've done. You ask because you need it. And the very next verse backs that up.

Close, but the song goes the other way. The writer asks, "If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand?" He isn't saying only the most faithful could stand. His question has no "except for these people" in it. Nobody could stand, and that's why the next verse matters so much.

Right, baker. The question is "…who, O Lord, could stand?" and the text never names a group of super-faithful folks who would pass. He asks it as a question with no one to point to. That leaves everybody needing what comes next, which is "…with You there is forgiveness…" (Psalm 130:4).

There it is, baker. "But with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared." That little word "But" turns the whole song around. The question in verse 3 was heavy, and verse 4 gives the answer. I'll take forgiveness over a perfect record any day.

I see the logic, since verse 3 does sound pretty heavy. But the song turns on one word: "But." Then it says, "…with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared." Forgiveness is what's with the LORD, friend, and that's the good news of this verse.

I can see why you'd pick it, down in the depths it can feel quiet. But look at how the song opens. The writer cries out, and then he says what is with the LORD: "But with You there is forgiveness…" He doesn't say the LORD is silent. He says the LORD forgives.

You got it, baker. "I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope." His hope isn't in a feeling or a plan. It's in what the LORD has said. That's a solid place to stand while the oven timer is still running.

Not quite, friend. The writer is in the depths, and nothing in the verse says he's leaning on himself. He says, "…in His word I put my hope." His hope rests on the LORD's word, not on how strong he feels. Honestly, my own strength never did much for my worn-out edges.
Walls are a fun guess, but this song never mentions any. Where he puts his hope is right there in verse 5: "…in His word I put my hope." It's the LORD's word, baker, and no brick is involved.

Baked right, baker. "My soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning…" Watchmen stand guard through the night, so I think morning is the thing they're counting on. He's saying his waiting is even more eager than theirs.

I can see rain on your mind, but the song picks a different picture. The verse says his soul waits "…more than watchmen wait for the morning…" Watchmen keep watch through the night, so I think the morning is what they're waiting for. Rain just isn't in the verse, friend.

A king is a big guess, baker, but it's not in this verse. The writer says his soul waits "…more than watchmen wait for the morning…" The picture is a night watch and the morning that ends it. No crown anywhere.

explanations.answer: Loving devotion and redemption are with Him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. "…for with the LORD is loving devotion, and with Him is redemption in abundance." Notice the reason isn't about anything Israel did. It's about who the LORD is and what is with Him. Redemption in ABUNDANCE, friend. That's not a stingy batch.

explanations.answer: Their enemies have already been defeated
explanations.explanation: Good guess for a hope-in-the-LORD kind of verse, but enemies never come up in this song. The reason he gives is "…for with the LORD is loving devotion, and with Him is redemption in abundance." The hope rests on the LORD's own loving devotion and redemption, baker.

explanations.answer: Their harvest will be bigger than ever
explanations.explanation: Bigger harvest, I like the optimism, but that's not in this song. His reason is "…for with the LORD is loving devotion, and with Him is redemption in abundance." The word "abundance" is there, but it belongs to redemption, friend, not to crops.

True, baker. "And He will redeem Israel from all iniquity." Look at that word "all." After a song that started in the depths, it ends with the LORD redeeming and no iniquity left out. That's a long way up from the bottom.

I get the hesitation after a song that starts so low, baker. But the song ends with this: "And He will redeem Israel from all iniquity." It really does say the LORD will redeem, and it really does say "all." So this one is true.

Yes, baker. David says, "My heart is not proud, O LORD, my eyes are not haughty." He's telling the LORD where his heart stands, and that's some humble talk. Me, I'd have been tempted to mention the hat.

Tired is a fair guess, since we've all been there. But David's words are "My heart is not proud, O LORD, my eyes are not haughty." The word that pairs with "haughty" is "proud." Same neighborhood, friend, and nobody mentions sleep.

Heavy fits the mood of Psalm 130, I'll give you that. But this is David in Psalm 131, and he says, "My heart is not proud, O LORD, my eyes are not haughty." The word is "proud," baker, and it matches "haughty" right beside it.

Not this time, baker. David says the opposite: "I do not aspire to great things or matters too lofty for me." He isn't telling the LORD he goes after the big stuff. He's telling Him he doesn't aspire to it.
Right, baker. David says, "I do not aspire to great things or matters too lofty for me." He's not reaching for things beyond him. And he says it straight to the LORD, which makes it even better.

explanations.answer: A weaned child with his mother
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David says, "like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me." It's a quiet picture, a child who is simply with his mother. I think that's about as calm as a soul can look.

That one's from another psalm, baker. In Psalm 23:2, David says the LORD "leads me beside quiet waters." But here in Psalm 131:2 the picture is different: "like a weaned child with his mother…" Same writer, different picture.

explanations.answer: A ship on a calm sea
explanations.explanation: Calm sea is a pretty picture, but it isn't David's. He says, "like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me." There are no boats in this psalm, friend. Just a child, and his mother right there.

You got it, baker. David closes with "O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, both now and forevermore." That covers today and every day after. Hope with no expiration date beats any coupon I've ever seen.
A harvest is a season, and David's call doesn't stop at one. He says, "…put your hope in the LORD, both now and forevermore." Forevermore goes way past any harvest, baker.

explanations.answer: As long as the temple stands
explanations.explanation: That's a clever guess, but David gives no condition at all. The verse says, "…put your hope in the LORD, both now and forevermore." No "as long as" in it, friend. Just now, and forevermore.
